passages.t: A word to Zedekiah as the last towns hold out
passages.happening:
As Nebuchadnezzar and all his army and the peoples of his empire fight against Jerusalem and its towns (verse 1), God sends Jeremiah to Zedekiah. The city will be handed to the king of Babylon and burned (verse 2). Zedekiah himself will not escape. He will see the king of Babylon face to face and go to Babylon (verse 3).

Yet God says of him, you will not die by the sword (verse 4). ‘You will die in peace’ (verse 5). As spices were burned for the kings before him, so people will burn spices for him and lament him (verse 5).

Jeremiah tells all this to Zedekiah in Jerusalem (verse 6), while the army of Babylon fights against Jerusalem and the remaining towns of Judah, Lachish and Azekah, for these alone of Judah's fortified cities still held out (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The siege began in Zedekiah's ninth year and ended in 587 or 586 BC. Verse 7 says only Lachish and Azekah still stood. Lachish was Judah's second city, about thirty miles southwest of Jerusalem, and Azekah lay to its north.

Clay letters found at Lachish in the 1930s, written by an officer at an outpost in those last months, survive. One says they are watching for the fire signals of Lachish and cannot see Azekah. Many scholars take that to mean Azekah had already fallen. The verse and the letter describe the same collapse from two sides.

Burning spices for a dead king was a royal honor at burial.
passages.later: Kings tells what became of Zedekiah: he was taken to the king of Babylon at Riblah and then to Babylon (2 Kings 25:6-7). Chronicles says Zedekiah ‘did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet’ (2 Chronicles 36:12).
passages.hard:
Jeremiah promised Zedekiah he would die in peace, but 52:10-11 says the Babylonians killed his sons before his eyes, blinded him and kept him in prison until he died. How does that fit?

Interpreters answer in different ways. Many read verses 4 and 5 as conditional: a peaceful death with royal honors was offered to Zedekiah if he surrendered, as Jeremiah later urged (38:17-18), and he did not. Others take it more narrowly: Zedekiah did not die by the sword but in captivity, and he may have been mourned by the exiles, which is all the verse strictly says. Still others note that verse 3, captured, taken to Babylon, seeing the king face to face, came true exactly, and verses 4 and 5 soften without cancelling it. The first reading fits the book's pattern of warnings that depend on the hearer's response.
passages.asks: Zedekiah was offered a better end and did not take it. Ask whether there is an offer of mercy in your life that depends on a choice you have not made. And ask what it means to see the end coming and still be given a word of grace.

passages.happening:
During the siege King Zedekiah made a covenant with all the people of Jerusalem to proclaim liberty (verse 8), that everyone should free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, and no one keep a fellow Judean in bondage (verse 9). All the officials and people agreed and set them free (verse 10). ‘But later they changed their minds and took back the menservants and maidservants they had freed’ (verse 11).

God reminds them of the covenant he made with their fathers when he brought them out of Egypt, the house of slavery (verse 13): every seventh year each must free a Hebrew who had sold himself into service (verse 14). They had just done what was right and made a covenant in God's house (verse 15). ‘But now you have changed your minds and profaned My name’ (verse 16).

So God proclaims liberty for them, to the sword, plague and famine (verse 17). Those who broke the covenant he will treat ‘like the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces’ (verse 18). The officials, priests and people who walked between the pieces will be handed to their enemies (verses 19 and 20). Zedekiah and his officials will be handed over too, and the Babylonian army that has withdrawn will come back, take the city and burn it (verses 21 and 22).
passages.hearers:
The slavery in view was debt servitude. A poor Israelite could sell himself into service to pay a debt, and the law said he must be freed after six years. Judah had long ignored that law. Under siege, the people freed their slaves.

Then, verse 21 explains, the Babylonian army withdrew. An Egyptian army under Pharaoh Hophra had marched out, and the Babylonians broke off the siege to meet it. In that lull, the owners took their slaves back. The danger seemed over, so the promise was dropped.

The calf cut in two was an ancient way of making a covenant. Those swearing walked between the halves, in effect calling down the same fate on themselves if they broke their word. God now holds them to their own oath.

The chapter describes a practice of its time and condemns those who broke faith with the people they had freed. It is no endorsement of slavery.
passages.later: The law said a Hebrew servant ‘in the seventh year you must set him free’ (Deuteronomy 15:12). God himself once passed between the pieces when he made his covenant with Abram (Genesis 15:17).
passages.asks: The people freed their slaves when they were afraid and took them back when the danger passed. Ask what promise you made to God in a crisis and forgot once it was over. And ask whom you hold in some kind of bondage that you could set free.
